title: Glider Performance Tool
text:
Comparing the PAM-equipped gliders of the NOAA Fisheries Glider Rodeo 2026 across mission modes: how each platform was piloted, how well it navigated, how long its battery and storage last, and how much noise it makes.
Seven gliders from four platform types flew the same trackline off the coast of Hawaii in January–February 2026:

title: Glider Performance Tool
text:
Approach

Split each deployment by rodeo mission mode (fast, slow, intermediate, drift, mini-rodeo).
Compute the same performance metrics for every glider.
Compare platforms and modes.

See Project Info for goals and datasets, and Glider Performance for what every glider actually did during the rodeo.

    Endurance is battery capacity by chemistry and bay
    (550 / 800 Ah primary, 215 / 300 Ah rechargeable) divided by total Ah per day, where the
    glider-and-standard-sensor load comes from the workbook's component power model and the
    external payload is added on top. Distance assumes 20 km/day.
    The external payload is read from content/data/extra-sensors.csv rather than
    from the workbook, so a sensor can be added, removed or re-costed by editing one line in the
    repository. The workbook hardcoded the same four inside a single formula; the replacement is
    checked against it on every build. Figures marked * carry a note
    — hover the name to read it.
    The workbook also reports a bare-glider endurance from the same power model. It is not
    shown here: it excludes the external sensors, so on these defaults it reads about five times
    longer and answers a different question.

title: Project Info
text:
Goals
Answer, for every glider and mission mode:

Piloting: how do pilots achieve each mission mode (pitch, buoyancy, dive depth, yos per surfacing)?
Navigation: how well does each glider hold the trackline, and how is that affected by currents?
Endurance: how does mission mode affect battery use and data storage?
Noise: how much self-noise (pumping, motors, flow) does each glider make?

title: Glider Performance
text:
Every glider in the rodeo flew the same plan: a shakedown, then fast,
slow, intermediate and drift blocks, then a short
repeat of slow, intermediate and fast at the end (the mini-modes, right of the hairline in each
panel). Because the modes are shared, the differences below are differences between the
platforms, not between missions. Numbers come from
output/glider_performance_summary.xlsx; each panel keeps its own y-axis, because a watt
and a cubic centimetre do not belong on one scale.



  
    Gliders
  
  
    Modes
  
  
    Metrics
  




Tradeoff explorer

The mission modes exist to answer what speed costs. Put one metric on each axis and every
glider-mode combination becomes a point, so the shape of the tradeoff shows up directly. Connect
the modes to follow one glider through the plan.


  
    X
    Y
     Connect modes
  
  
    Presets
  



Ranking

Every glider-mode combination on one metric, sorted. This is the view for “who used the least
energy per kilometre” — and for seeing how much of the spread is the platform and how much
is the mode it was flying.


  
    Metric
  



Mode comparison

The same numbers as a grid: one row per glider, one column per mode. Gaps are combinations with no
data rather than zeroes.


  
    Metric
  



Data recorded

How much raw data each system actually wrote during the rodeo. The deployments were not the same
length, so the per-day figure is the fairer comparison between PAM systems — and the spread is
mostly channel count and sample rate, not platform.


  
    Total recordedGB
    
    
  
  
    Recording rateGB/day
    
    Total raw data divided by the length of that glider’s deployment.
  


Efficiency

Two sections above ask what a kilometre cost and how much each system recorded. This divides
one by the other: how far a glider went, and how much it wrote, for every kilowatt‑hour it
spent. Up and to the right is more of both for the same energy. Neither axis is the
answer — a platform can buy data with distance, and the fastest way to look efficient on
the vertical axis is to record at a high bit rate.




The numbers

Every value on this page, for the gliders, modes and metrics selected above. Hover is a
convenience; this table is the source.

title: Seaglider Endurance Calculation
text:
Predicts how long a Seaglider will last on a given mission. Kongsberg publishes
  no endurance tool for firmware 66.12, so this one is fitted to our own gliders' logs:
  every dive's per-device on-times and currents from SG644 (2018, 2019, 2022) and SG150 (2021),
  1,500+ dives in all. Run against those dives, it reproduces each
  mission's logged energy to within a few percent (see How well it fits).

  How well it fits
  Each logged dive run through the model using only what a pilot plans with: the
  dive's depth and duration, surface time, $MAX_BUOY, $SM_CC, the data it sent and its sensor
  settings. The model's total against what the glider logged, mission by mission.
  
    Energy per mission: logged against model
    Logged by the gliderModel
    
    
  
  
    
  

  What the logs showed
  
    
      The glider's battery counter leaves the PAM out
      SG644's $24V_AH counter books every device except the PAM recorder. The CF card's
      BATTERY tally for mission 5 (to 3 July 2018) lists 45 Ah drawn by the PAM,
      and the counter's 247.6 Ah equals the tally without it. The recorder's
      PAM.CNF puts it on the 15 V main line, so the pack gave
      ~293 Ah of 310 while the glider reported 248.
      This calculator counts the PAM. When a PAM is fitted, add its time to the glider's
      counter before trusting the remaining capacity.
    
    
      SciCon or TT8: which is cheaper
      With the CT, optode and SeaOWL on the SciCon sampling every ~10 s, the SciCon
      averaged 25 mA for all of it. Polled by the TT8 instead, the glider charges each
      sensor its .cnf current for every second it is powered, and keeps the TT8
      awake ~3 s per sensor-second. The Contros optode's .cnf says 300 mA for
      2.8 s a sample: 845 mAs, ~3.6× what the SciCon drew for all its sensors over a 10 s cycle. On mission 6's dives, without the PAM, that is ~88 days on the SciCon against ~44 on the TT8.
      The SciCon reports its own consumption; the TT8 figure is the glider's bookkeeping.
      Part of the gap may be a conservative .cnf rating, so a bench measurement of the optode
      would settle it. Until then, edit a sensor's mA to try a measured value.
    
    
      What moves endurance most
      The echosounder. In 2022 it logged 400 mA for the whole dive: 0.77 Ah per dive,
      more than everything else together, which is why that mission ran at 16.5 Ah/day against
      2.6–4.5 in the SciCon years.
      The pump, then depth. A cc pumped at apogee costs 13 J plus 0.021 J per metre
      of depth, so ~15 J at 100 m and ~34 J at 1000 m. Volume is (MAX_BUOY + SM_CC)
      per dive. SG644 pumped 1.22× that in 2022, at a lower pack voltage (12.4 V against
      13.4 V in 2018).
    
    
      The earlier spreadsheet
      endurance calc.xlsx fitted per-device factors to 92 dives of one
      deployment, and its pump term already scaled with MAX_BUOY + SM_CC. For its own
      settings (990 m, T_DIVE 420, CT and optode on the SciCon) it and this model agree on the
      energy of a dive: 0.51 Ah there, 0.50 Ah here.
      The endurance differs because it fixed every dive at 2 h. At T_DIVE 420 a 990 m dive
      takes about 7 h, so 303 Ah lasts ~180 days, not 49. It also scaled Iridium and the motors
      by 0.5 and the pump by 0.3 by hand, and added the CTD and O2 on top of the SciCon, which
      already includes them. Those roughly cancelled out.
    
  

  Missions in the archive
  
    
  

  
    How it is built. code/extract_seaglider_dives.py reduces the
    deployment archive (the basestation's per-dive netCDF files, 1.6 GB, kept outside the
    repository) to one row per dive in content/data/seaglider-dives.csv.
    code/fit_seaglider_model.py fits each group of loads against what drives it:
    the pump against volume and depth, the motors against dive time, the processor against
    cycle time, Iridium against data sent, and the SciCon against its sample rate. The fit is
    written to content/data/seaglider-model.json.
    node code/build_seaglider_page.js runs code/seaglider_model.js
    on every dive, fails if any mission misses by more than 25%, and only then updates this
    page. Fitted on 2018 alone, the model predicted the 2022 mission, with different sensors
    and no SciCon, to within 7%.
    Limits. Everything is calibrated on two gliders on firmware 66.12. Depths beyond
    1000 m, and anything past 300 m for SG150, are extrapolation. The SeaOWL's cost on the
    TT8 is estimated, since it only ever flew on the SciCon. The Kongsberg (iRobot) Seaglider
    Mission Endurance Estimator user guide (doc. 4366008) was used for parameter names and the
    rule that a dual-pack glider lasts as long as its weaker pack.

        ~Duration is derived. It assumes constant horizontal speed and an even division of route distance among gliders.
        !Not an operational plan. Currents, bathymetry, energy use, station keeping, and deployment logistics are not modeled.
        +Geometry is reproducible. Area, transect count, and route length are calculated directly from the polygon and generated tracks.
      
      
        Calculation assumptions
        
          Transects are generated at the selected compass orientation and clipped to the study polygon.
          For the lawnmower option, transect segments are alternated and connected in sequence; connector distance is included.
          Nominal travel rate is speed in knots × 1.852 km/nmi × 24 h/day.
          Dive-cycle horizontal distance is approximated as 2 × target depth / tan(glide angle), assuming a symmetric straight-line descent and ascent.
          Map dots represent estimated surfacing locations, not subsurface profile positions or commanded waypoints.
          With multiple gliders, route distance is divided evenly among vehicles for the duration estimate only; tracks are not yet spatially assigned to individual gliders.
